scenes.tts: They met in the dissection hall at Prague and recognized each other at once as the same kind of person. They married, came to the United States in 1922, and ran into the rules of the era head-on: a Buffalo institute director ordered Gerty to stop publishing with her husband, and she refused; at Washington University she was hired at a tenth of Carl's salary for sixteen years under nepotism rules.

scenes.tts: The Cori cycle came out of work they did on the side of the tumor metabolism they were paid to study: muscle breaks glucose to lactate, the blood carries the lactate to the liver, and the liver spends energy to rebuild glucose.

scenes.tts: Chasing a fraction everyone else discarded, they found the glycogen debranching enzyme, and Gerty read its chromatography spot instantly and ran down the hall shouting, "It's free glucose, it's free glucose!" — the same free glucose that this chapter's last enzyme, glucose-6-phosphatase, releases to the blood.

scenes.tts: She went further, matching the wrong-shaped glycogen in sick children to specific missing enzymes: the first proof that one broken enzyme can cause an inherited disease.

scenes.tts: When the Nobel came in 1947, Carl used the banquet to center Gerty. The same year, dying of the myelofibrosis she had worked through for a decade, she was finally made a full professor.
